The eight-string guitar is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.322-5, sounding with eight vibrating strings; its construction is close to the six- and seven-string guitar, and both hollow and solid designs exist. Players can use non-standard tunings to widen the range, for example major-thirds tuning; the nineteenth-century Italian players Giulio Regondi and Luigi Legnani used guitars of this kind. Today it appears in classical, jazz and heavy metal playing, and bands such as Meshuggah and Animals as Leaders have increased its use.
八弦吉他起源於19世紀非標準吉他，義大利演奏者Giulio Regondi與Lu: The eight-string guitar began with the non-standard guitars of the nineteenth century, used by the Italian players Giulio Regondi and Luigi Legnani. In the middle of the twentieth century Ralph Patt developed major-thirds tuning for jazz improvisation and asked a luthier to convert a six-string hollow guitar to eight strings; Roy Connors also converted an eight-string and took out an American patent. In 1994 Paul Galbraith worked with David Rubio on the design of an eight-string classical guitar. The eight-string electric guitar then spread through its use by metal bands, and in the past dozen years or so it has extended beyond classical, jazz and metal.
